title: Envy, stinginess and regret
carry: envy pushes away; harbored thoughts keep it fed

cards: A text arrives from an old classmate. She got the job, the one both of them applied for. The reply goes out fast: congratulations, three exclamation points, a party emoji.
And underneath the exclamation points, something small turns its face away. Yesterday's family leaned toward things. Today's family leans the other way.
The Abhidhamma has a name for that turning away, and it gives it three relatives, one of which is a surprise.

teach.b: The head of this family is dosa, aversion: not toward, but away. In the Abhidhamma it covers the whole range, from fury down to a mild ugh: irritation, dread, sulking, the small flinch at a voice in the next room.

The Abhidhammattha Sangaha gives it three relatives that appear only in its company. Envy, issa: the mind that can't bear someone else's good fortune. Stinginess, macchariya: the mind that can't bear sharing its own.

teach.h: ENVY WATCHES THEIRS; STINGINESS GUARDS MINE.
teach.b: Envy watches their plate; stinginess guards mine. Both push something away, so the manual seats them with aversion, not with greed.
The third relative is kukkucca, regret, or worry: brooding over a thing done that shouldn't have been, or a thing left undone that should have been. Regret can sound like conscience.
But in this list, the stewing kind is a pushing against the past, aversion turned back on oneself. Seeing a mistake clearly and making amends is a different matter. What keeps this family fed?

The Dhammapada answers near its start, in Max Müller's words: "'He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,'--in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease." Harbor is the telling word.
A harbor is where boats are tied up and kept. Envy works the same way: one comparison, tied up and replayed. Regret too: one evening, docked and visited every night.
In a few days this path meets the factor the tradition sets against envy, gladness at someone else's good.

how: Abhidhamma students learn aversion, envy, stinginess and regret as the hate-group of unwholesome factors, and in some Buddhist communities people meet envy by deliberately rejoicing in others' good fortune.

o: the hatred that holds back a whole community
aversion with envy, stinginess and regret
anger handed down from parents to children

p: envy: can't bear their good fortune

s: in the manual, envy belongs with greed
envy pushes away another's good fortune, so the manual seats it with aversion.
brooding over what was done or left undone is a pushing against the past.
it covers everything from fury down to a small ugh.

games.q: a friend gets the thing you both wanted, and you notice a small tightening. by the manual's map, what is it?
o: envy: aversion to her good fortune.
games.why: the manual seats envy in aversion's family: not so much wanting her thing as pushing away her good fortune.

practice: If you'd like, gently bring to mind someone who has something you'd like, a job, a home, an ease, a gift for something, and watch the very first moment for a small tightening, a turning away.

If it's there, that's envy, and it's only a moment; don't scold it, just feel where it sits. Then, if you can, add one plain thought, good for them, even if it isn't fully meant, and see what happens to the tightness.

wordCard.voice: Aversion's family. Aversion, envy, stinginess and regret: four ways the mind pushes away. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali issa: envy, the mind that can't bear another's good fortune.

carryVoice: Your line: envy pushes away; harbored thoughts keep it fed. It doesn't need new reasons; it lives on the ones already kept. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: 'He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,'--in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.

sources.ref: Abhidhammattha Sangaha, ch. 2 (the hate group: dosa, issa, macchariya, kukkucca)
